source.title: Induction Signatures Are Not Enough: A Matched-Compute Study of Load-Bearing Structure in In-Context Learning

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites work on copy suppression but its own experiments concern forward induction circuitry and synthetic copy-data curricula. It does not test the stated copy-suppression claims. Its induction-head ablation results are related findings recorded under fits_no_version.
record.gate_note: No direct results test L10H7, copy suppression’s share of loss, calibration from copy suppression, self-repair via copy suppression, or whether negative heads in other settings share that role. The paper does measure and ablate forward-induction heads; those results concern a related but different construct and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites McDougall et al. (2023) only in related work and the glossary. Its experiments train new 0.13B–1B models with synthetic copy snippets and measure forward induction and anti-induction head scores, ICL and perplexity. It never examines L10H7, GPT-2 small, negative or copy-suppression heads, calibration from suppression, or self-repair. Its induction-head ablations concern a different construct (forward copying, not suppression of copying).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Bi-Induct amplifies induction signatures but does not consistently improve ICL. The 1B natural-only model performs best on function probes and is most ablation-sensitive. The authors conclude that eliciting a mechanism is not the same as making it load-bearing.
record.recipe_differences: The original analyzes copy suppression in GPT-2 small using head-level circuit and loss-effect methods. This paper trains new 0.13B–1B models with synthetic forward/backward copy snippets and evaluates induction telemetry, few-shot ICL, and targeted induction-head ablations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ablation effect varies by model scale and training curriculum; the largest relative ICL drops occur in natural-only models. Telemetry also varies with scale and mix ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing the top-2% induction-scoring heads per layer cut function-probe ICL by 4.9–22.6%. Matched random-head ablation changed it by −4.2% to +17.0%. Drops were largest in natural-only models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forward-induction heads are causally load-bearing for function-style ICL, and natural-only training concentrates this reliance more than synthetic copy-snippet curricula.

record.problems: The paper states that mechanistic analysis is limited to final checkpoints and models up to 1B parameters. Table 3 gives no uncertainty values for the ablation deltas, although experiments are described as averaging across three seeds elsewhere. The results concern induction rather than copy suppression and therefore do not directly establish the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Induction telemetry and few-shot curriculum comparisons were not cataloged as separate rows because they do not test a claim version; the directly related targeted-ablation results and their random-ablation comparisons are included.

untested.parts: No analysis of GPT-2 small L10H7 or of any head suppressing predicted and in-context tokens.
No QK/OV analysis of a suppression head and no loss-effect decomposition.
Perplexity is a training-quality guardrail; there is no calibration test tied to copy suppression.
No upstream-copier ablation and no measurement of compensation by a suppression head.
No negative heads are identified in the trained models, and none are compared with copy suppression.

record.verdict_notes: The row states (observed/partial/absent) describe induction-ablation effect sizes, not any copy-suppression version; all rows correctly carry versions ["none"]. Rows r13–r24 are random-ablation controls. The paper's anti-induction (backward copy) scores are not copy suppression and stay near zero.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test L10H7 or whether suppression is its main role across the training distribution.
No QK/OV circuit analysis of copy suppression or loss-effect decomposition is reported.
Held-out perplexity is used as a language-modeling quality guardrail, not as a test of calibration improvement from copy suppression.
No upstream copier ablation or copy-suppression self-repair test is reported.
The paper studies forward induction heads, not whether negative heads in narrow tasks or other models instantiate copy suppression.
No distribution-wide analysis of self-repair mechanisms is reported.

relation.reason: Copy suppression appears as background in related work and the glossary; the study provides no copy-suppression experiment.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure forward/backward copy telemetry and induction-head dependence of ICL, without testing or using any listed copy-suppression version.

source_check.notes: All values are relative percentage changes from each model's clean run, not percentage-point changes. The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased; backward copying and copy suppression remain distinct constructs.
